title: How Exactly Do You Spend Your Time
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece sets out a specific diagnostic, the Time Audit or Time Field, and is unusually precise about its mechanics. The instruction is to log activity in 30-minute increments across two weeks, in real time rather than from memory, on the grounds that recall of what happened hours earlier is worse than people assume. The step the essay treats as most important is the second one: assigning each completed increment a satisfaction value while the feeling is still fresh, which turns a time log into something evaluative rather than merely descriptive. It also asks for restraint, holding off on conclusions until the full two weeks have elapsed. The framing device is a shift from spending to investing time, and the essay is concrete about which activities it counts as investments: exercise, meaningful work, learning, and deepening relationships, on the test that they pay in both the present and the future. It closes by recommending a doubling-down on learning, with Franklin on knowledge paying the best interest.
points: The method is specified precisely enough to run: 30-minute increments, logged in real time, across two full weeks, because retrospective reconstruction of a day is less accurate than people assume.
The step treated as most important is scoring each increment for satisfaction within the day, which converts a time log from a record into a diagnostic.
A deliberate restraint is built in, no strong conclusions until the two weeks are complete, guarding against acting on an unrepresentative few days.
The spend-versus-invest reframe supplies the decision rule, with investments defined as activities paying dividends in both the present and the future.
The named investment categories, exercise, meaningful work, learning and deepening relationships, give the audit something to reallocate toward rather than just something to feel bad about.
quotes: Spending too much of the day on activities that do not produce happiness, satisfaction, or productivity is a common affliction.
Known as a Time Audit or Time Field, the idea is to document how you spend your time in 30-minute increments over two weeks.
Trying to remember what you did hours earlier is harder than you think. So the key is to track your activities in real time.
After you complete a given day’s Time Field, the next step, and perhaps the most important, is to assign each 30-minute increment a value for satisfaction.
Every day is rich with time until you make choices that either invest or spend those resources.
Activities such as exercise, producing meaningful work, learning new things, and deepening relationships create value now and into the future.
